scene.testo: Four hundred miles above your head, a crew of astronauts is orbiting Earth at 17,500 mph. They circle the planet 16 times a day. And between the experiments and repairs, they still find time to play. Here is how.

Imagine you are floating inside the International Space Station. It is 6 AM, Greenwich time, the clock the crew follows. Nothing under your feet. Nothing holding you down. Your sleeping bag is strapped to the wall, and your arms drift upward like seaweed.

You unzip the bag and push off gently. One finger is enough. You glide down the module like a swimmer without water. Every astronaut learns this on day one. Moving slowly is the secret. Move fast, and you will bounce off a wall.

Here is the surprise. Astronauts do have free time. The schedule on the station runs about 16 hours a day for work, and the crew sleeps about eight hours. Weekends are lighter. And on those days, the fun begins.

So what is the first thing most astronauts do? They look out the window. The station has a dome called the Cupola, with seven windows. It faces straight down at Earth, about 250 miles below your feet.

Through that glass, the planet slides past at 17,500 mph. Oceans, deserts, and storms roll by in minutes. At night, you see city lights glowing orange like spilled embers. Astronauts have said they could watch it for hours.
And because the station circles Earth every 90 minutes or so, you get a sunrise or a sunset roughly every 45 minutes. That is about 16 sunrises every single day. Imagine trying to sleep through that.

Many astronauts take photographs. They use real cameras with long lenses, and they shoot hundreds of images. Some of the most famous pictures of Earth were taken by crew members during their own free time, floating at the window.
Now let us talk about food. Dinner is often a social event. The crew floats around one table, strapping their feet or holding on to the edge. Everything is packaged, and everything has to stay put.

A meal might include rehydrated pasta, a thermostabilized entree, or tortillas. Why tortillas? Because bread makes crumbs. And crumbs in zero gravity do not fall. They float into your eyes, your nose, and the air filters.

Drinks come in sealed pouches with a straw. Open a cup, and the liquid forms a wobbling ball. Astronauts have shown on camera how a floating blob of water can be caught with a spoon, or even with the mouth.

Here is a favorite treat. Crews have celebrated holidays and birthdays on board. Special food packages arrive on cargo ships. Families can send small gifts too. A birthday cake is not allowed, because of those crumbs. But a pouch of something sweet works.

In December 2013, NASA reported that crew members on the station put up a small holiday tree and shared a festive dinner. The tree was tiny, and everything was tied down. But the spirit was the same as at home.

Next, the gym. This may not sound like fun, but many astronauts say they enjoy it. They have to exercise about two hours every day. Without gravity, bones and muscles weaken fast. So the gym is a daily must.
There is a treadmill, a stationary bike, and a weight machine. On the treadmill, you wear a harness with straps that pull you down onto the belt. Otherwise, you would simply float off with each step.

In April 2016, astronaut Tim Peake ran the London Marathon from the station. NASA and the European Space Agency both reported it. He covered 26.2 miles on the treadmill, strapped in, in about three hours and 35 minutes.

That is the same distance as a marathon on Earth, roughly 460 football fields laid end to end. Imagine running that while orbiting at 17,500 mph and watching Earth slide by. Few runners have ever had that view.

Now to the really fun part. Play. Astronauts love to play with weightlessness itself. They flip, they spin, and they race each other down the length of a module. One push, and you fly like a superhero.

Crews have filmed themselves doing somersaults, spinning like tops, and pushing off walls to see who can fly farthest. A good push can carry you the whole length of a module in a few seconds, without touching anything.

There is a classic trick, too. Astronauts toss food into the air and catch it with their mouths. Candy, grapes, and small snacks float in a straight line, never curving down. NASA footage has shown crews doing just that.

Then there is hair. In zero gravity, long hair floats up and out in every direction. Astronauts have shown clips of their hair standing straight like a lion's mane. Washing it takes special rinseless shampoo and a lot of towels.

Water experiments are another favorite. In 2013, Canadian astronaut Chris Hadfield showed how wringing out a wet washcloth in space makes the water cling to the cloth and crawl up his hands, forming a tube around his arms.

The same astronaut also played a guitar on board. He recorded a music video of David Bowie's Space Oddity, and it was released on May 12, 2013. Millions of people watched it. It is one of the best known things anyone ever did on the station.

Music is common up there. Astronauts bring instruments, such as guitars, flutes, and keyboards. A small keyboard fits in a locker. Playing together is a way to feel like a team, and a way to feel like home.

Movie night is a tradition too. The crew gathers around a laptop, floats side by side, and watches a film together. They have said they pick comedies, classics, and sometimes space movies, just to compare notes with reality.

They also read books, play video games, and listen to podcasts. The station has an internet link, so crews can send emails and browse the web, though the connection is slower than what you have at home.

Staying connected matters most. Astronauts can make video calls to their families. Some phone calls go to the ground through a radio link. A child's voice from Earth, heard 250 miles up, means more than any gadget.

Crews also talk to schoolchildren. NASA arranges live calls between astronauts and classrooms. A student asks a question, and an astronaut floats in front of the camera to answer, sometimes flipping upside down to prove a point.

Some astronauts also use amateur radio. Through a program called ARISS, they can talk to students and hobbyists on the ground. The contact lasts about 10 minutes, the time the station is in range as it passes overhead.

Now the most thrilling activity of all. Not every astronaut gets a spacewalk, but those who do describe it as unforgettable. Outside, the temperature swings from about minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in shadow to plus 250 in sunlight.

A spacewalk is work, not play. Astronauts repair, install, and maintain equipment. But many say the view is pure joy. You float outside with Earth below you, held only by a tether. Some walks last more than six hours.

Even work can have a playful side. Astronauts sign their suits, bring small mascots, and sometimes carry personal items in their pockets. A small toy floating in the cabin is often a sign that a mission has just begun.

That tradition is real. When a crew launches, a small plush toy often floats in the cabin once the ship reaches orbit. It acts as a zero gravity indicator, a quick visual sign that the spacecraft has left the pull of the ground.

Science itself can be fun. Astronauts run experiments with fire, fluids, and plants. They have grown lettuce and zinnia flowers aboard the station. In January 2016, NASA reported that a zinnia bloomed in orbit, and the crew shared photos.

Tending plants is a calming hobby. Astronauts have said that watching something green grow reminds them of home. Crews have also eaten fresh lettuce grown on board, a rare treat after months of packaged meals.

Then there is sleep, which is a pleasure of its own. Each astronaut has a small private cabin, about the size of a phone booth. There is a sleeping bag, a laptop, and personal photos. And you sleep standing up, in a way.
In zero gravity there is no up. Your arms float in front of you. Sleeping bags are tied down so you do not drift into equipment. Many astronauts say they sleep deeply, and some report vivid dreams.

There are tough moments too. Months away from home can feel lonely. Astronauts say that small rituals help, such as a favorite meal, a call to a friend, or a quiet minute at the window watching the planet turn.

Compare that with life on Earth. You have a backyard, a couch, a dog, and a walk around the block. They have a space the size of a six bedroom house, shared with six or seven other people, for about six months.

The station weighs about one million pounds and measures about 357 feet end to end, roughly the length of a football field including the end zones. It is the largest structure humans have ever built in orbit.

And yet, inside, everyone knows each other's habits. Crews eat together, work together, and joke together. Laughter is part of the schedule. A good sense of humor, astronauts often say, matters as much as any technical skill.
So what do astronauts do for fun? They gaze at Earth, run marathons, play music, grow flowers, watch movies, and flip through the air. Their fun is simple, human, and a little bit weightless.

Here is the most surprising detail. The station has been continuously occupied since November 2, 2000. That means someone has been floating up there, playing, working, and watching sunrises, every single day for more than 20 years.

The next sunrise is only minutes away. Somewhere up there, an astronaut is pressing a face to the glass, smiling at 17,500 mph. Imagine that view. Now you know how they spend their free time. Subscribe to Orbital Days.

descrizione:
What do astronauts do for fun in space? From running a marathon on a treadmill to playing guitar, growing flowers, watching movies, and gazing at 16 sunrises a day, life aboard the International Space Station is full of surprising downtime.

In this documentary, you float inside the station at 6 AM, eat dinner without gravity, work out two hours a day, and learn how crews stay connected with family. Every fact comes from NASA, ESA, and the astronauts' own accounts.
